instrument.title: Expert study on generated Artemis exercises
instrument.materiality_rule: Answer **No** if the problem would plausibly cost a student at the target level noticeable time, lead to a wrong submission, or send them to a tutor. A cosmetic issue that does none of these is **Yes**.

pages.title: Purpose of the study
pages.body:
Thank you for taking part. We study how well an AI-based pipeline generates programming
exercises for Artemis. You will rate several exercises, each written for a different phase of
a course. Automated checks already cover correctness. We therefore ask for your view as an
instructor on the didactical quality of each exercise.

Neither you nor the other raters know which model generated the exercises. We store your
answers under a pseudonymous ID. Please do not discuss the exercises with anyone until we
inform you that the study has closed.

pages.title: How a rating works
pages.body:
You rate each exercise in four parts. Each part adds material:

| Part | You see | You rate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Brief, problem statement | Clarity |
| B | + template repository, diff between template and solution | Solvability, objective alignment, difficulty, scaffolding |
| C | + test names and failure messages | Feedback quality, readiness (first rating) |
| D | + automatic findings | The findings, readiness (second rating) |

The brief describes what the instructor asked for, including topic, target level, course
phase, and constraints. The diff shows what the student has to write, and you do not need to
check it line by line. The test overview shows only what students see in Artemis and does not
contain the test code. You cannot go back to an earlier part. If later material changes your
view, you can note this in the free-text field at the end.

pages.title: Answering the items
pages.body:
You answer each item with Yes or No, and a few items also offer N/A. If you answer No, please
note briefly where the problem is. For borderline cases, the materiality rule applies:

> Answer **No** if the problem would plausibly cost a student at the target level noticeable time, lead to a wrong submission, or send them to a tutor. A cosmetic issue that does none of these is **Yes**.

| Situation | Item | Answer | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| "recieve" is misspelled in the statement | CL2 | Yes | Cosmetic issue |
| The statement asks for the average, but the tests expect two decimal places rounded half up | SO1 | No | Leads to a wrong submission |
| The statement says "ignore invalid entries" without defining whether an empty name is invalid, and a test checks this case | CL1 | No | Two reasonable readings |
| The test `countsOnlyActiveMembers` fails with "expected: <3> but was: <0>" | FB1 | Yes | The test name explains the problem |
| Several tests are named `test1` to `test5` and have no messages | FB1 | No | The student cannot tell what is wrong |

pages.title: Meaning of the readiness levels
pages.body:
The readiness items ask how much work you would need to deploy the exercise to the target
students. The following examples serve as anchors:

| Level | Meaning | Typical example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 5: Deploy as is | No change needed | You would publish the exercise today. |
| 4: Minor edits | Wording or formatting of the statement only | You clarify a sentence or add the expected output format to the statement. |
| 3: Moderate edits | Local changes, the design stays | You add failure messages to a few tests, rename a misleading stub, or fix one rule and its test. |
| 2: Major revision | Parts must be redesigned | The template already solves the core concept, or half of the tasks have no tests. |
| 1: Discard | Writing from scratch is faster | The exercise targets a different topic or level. |

Please rate your own effort as an instructor. The other items cover the effort of students.

calibration.title: Practice exercise
calibration.intro: We do not analyse the practice exercise. It lets you practise the items and shows how we interpret them. Afterwards, the tool shows our answers and the reasons for them. If your answers differ, please read the explanations. You do not need to change anything.

items.prompt: Is every required behaviour stated so that only one reasonable reading exists?
items.look_for: a rule two competent students would implement differently ("sort the items" without key or direction, an inclusive or exclusive bound); an example whose result does not follow from the stated rule.

items.prompt: Do the statement and template tell the student everything needed to produce the expected results, without seeing the tests?
items.look_for: an edge case mentioned without its expected result; an output that must match exactly (message text, number format, ordering) but is not given verbatim.

items.prompt: Would a student who fails a test learn from its name and message what is wrong, without being handed the solution?
items.look_for: tests without a message, so the student sees only "expected: <3> but was: <0>"; names such as `test1`; messages that spell out the code to write.

items.prompt: How much work would it take you to deploy this exercise to students at the target level?

questionnaire.title: Rating
questionnaire.perspective: Answer as an instructor deciding whether to give this exercise to students at the target level and course phase stated in the brief.

parts.title: Problem statement
parts.opens: Open now: the brief and the problem statement.

items.prompt: Is every required behaviour stated so that only one reasonable reading exists?
items.look_for: a rule two competent students would implement differently ("sort the items" without key or direction, an inclusive or exclusive bound); an example whose result does not follow from the stated rule.

items.prompt: Is the statement easy to understand for a student at the target level?
items.look_for: undefined jargon; requirements buried in the narrative; a statement much longer or denser than the task warrants.

parts.title: Template and diff
parts.opens: Open now: the template repository and the diff between template and solution. Skimming the template is enough: which files are given, which stubs the student fills in, and what the comments say. The diff shows what the student has to add or change. You do not need to check it line by line.

items.prompt: Do the statement and template tell the student everything needed to produce the expected results, without seeing the tests?
items.look_for: an edge case mentioned without its expected result; an output that must match exactly (message text, number format, ordering) but is not given verbatim.

items.prompt: Does the exercise practise the concept or learning objective named in the brief?
Must the student actually apply the target concept to solve the task?
items.look_for: the concept is already implemented in the template; a plain approach solves the task equally well and the statement does not rule it out (a recursion task solvable with a simple loop).

options.label: N/A, the brief names no specific construct or technique

items.prompt: Does the exercise honour the explicit requirements of the brief?
items.look_for: a requested diagram, edge case, determinism constraint, given type, or audience that the exercise ignores.

items.prompt: Is the scenario sensible and motivating for the task?
items.look_for: a context bolted onto an unrelated computation; contrived rules presented as realistic; wrong domain facts; a scenario that excludes or stereotypes groups of students.

items.prompt: Are the difficulty and the amount of work appropriate for the target level and course phase?
items.note: Judge against the brief, the size facts in the header, and the diff.

choices.label: Too easy or too little work
Too hard or too much work

items.prompt: Does the template give the right amount of support, so that the student's effort goes to the target concept?
items.look_for: students must write boilerplate the exercise does not aim to teach (visible in the diff); so much is given that little remains; stubs whose purpose is unclear.

items.prompt: Do the tasks of the statement form useful steps, so that students see their partial progress?
items.look_for: one task for a multi-part exercise; a task that cannot be attempted before a later one; task titles that do not say what to do.
